item.title: Don't Measure Unit Test Code Coverage
item.author: emecas
item.description:
Don’t Measure Unit Test Code Coverage
By James Shore
01 Feb, 2019
https://www.jamesshore.com/v2/blog/2019/dont-measure-unit-test-code-coverage

If you’re using test-driven development, don’t measure unit test code coverage. It’s worse than a useless statistic; it will actively lead you astray.

What should you do instead? That depends on what you want to accomplish.

  • To improve code and test practices: perform root-cause analysis of escaped defects, then improve your design and process to prevent that sort of defect from happening again
  • To improve programmer code quality: teach testing skills, speed up the test loop, refactor more, use evolutionary design, and try pairing or mobbing
  • To improve test discipline: use coaching and discipline-enhancing practices such as pairing or mobbing
  • To add tests to legacy code: nurture a habit of adding tests as part of working on any code
  • To improve requirements code quality: involve customer representatives early in the process
  • To improve non-functional quality: use a mix of real-world monitoring, fail-fast code, and specialized testbeds
  • (TDD reflexion) Here’s the thing about TDD: any code you want to cover is ipso facto covered. If you’re still getting defects, something else is wrong.

Source: commit 659e7c7 in My-Notes, improved in 6cc6d0e (2026-11-23).
